section.title: The King of Glory
section.sectionRationale: A processional entrance liturgy, likely sung as the ark of the covenant was carried up to Zion, moving from a declaration of God's ownership of the whole earth, through the same entrance question asked in Psalm 15, to a triumphant, antiphonal call for the ancient gates to lift up their heads so the King of glory may enter. Its closing question and answer, 'Who is this King of glory', has been read since the earliest church as anticipating Christ's ascension and enthronement.
section.thesis: The earth and everyone in it belongs to the LORD who alone may ascend His holy hill with clean hands and a pure heart, and the psalm's climactic call for the ancient gates to admit the King of glory anticipates the triumphant entrance and enthronement of Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the LORD's ownership of the whole earth; the entrance question of who may ascend His holy hill, answered by clean hands and a pure heart; and the closing antiphonal call for the gates to lift up their heads so the King of glory may enter.

verses.text: The earth is the LORD's, and the fullness thereof, the world and all who dwell therein.
For He has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the waters.

units.label: Who may ascend the hill of the Lord?

verses.text: Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place?

He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to an idol 
or swear deceitfully.
He will receive blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation.
Such is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O God of Jacob. {{selah|Selah}}

units.label: Lift up your heads, O gates

verses.text:
Lift up your heads, O gates! Be lifted up, O ancient doors, 
that the {{kavod|King of Glory}} may enter!

Who is this King of Glory? The LORD strong and mighty, 
the LORD mighty in battle.

Lift up your heads, O gates! Be lifted up, O ancient doors, 
that the King of Glory may enter!
Who is He, this King of Glory? The LORD of Hosts, He is the King of Glory. Selah

selah.gloss: A musical or liturgical notation of uncertain precise meaning, likely marking a pause, rest, or moment for reflection or instrumental interlude within the psalm's singing.

kavod.gloss: Glory, weight, splendor, the visible weightiness of God's presence and majesty. The 'King of kavod' is the King whose very presence carries the weight of divine glory, a title the New Testament applies to the risen and ascended Christ, 1 Corinthians 2:8, James 2:1.

basic.context: This psalm opens by declaring that the whole earth and everyone in it belongs to the LORD, its Creator and founder. It then asks the same searching entrance question found in Psalm 15, who may ascend God's holy hill, and answers with a portrait of clean hands and a pure heart. The psalm closes with a dramatic, likely antiphonal, procession scene: a call for the ancient gates themselves to lift up their heads so the King of glory may enter, followed by the question, repeated twice, 'Who is this King of glory', answered each time by naming the LORD, strong, mighty, and the LORD of Hosts.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm was likely composed for a specific historical procession, perhaps when David brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 6, but its closing scene of gates opening for the entering King of glory has, from the earliest church onward, been read as prophetically pointing beyond that original event to Christ's ascension and enthronement, without denying its original historical setting.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm marks its central turning points with selah, and its climactic title for God, the King of kavod, glory, describes the visible weightiness of divine majesty entering through gates that are called to lift up their heads, a title later applied by the New Testament directly to the risen and glorified Christ.
basic.typology: The ancient gates and doors commanded to lift up their heads for the entering King of glory function as a type of the heavens themselves opening to receive the ascending, exalted Christ, and of every barrier that must yield before His rightful lordship.
basic.christ: The early church consistently read this psalm's triumphant procession as anticipating Christ's ascension, the true King of glory entering into heaven's gates after His resurrection. Paul calls Jesus 'the Lord of glory' using this exact title, 1 Corinthians 2:8, and James similarly names Him 'the Lord of glory', James 2:1, applying this psalm's climactic title directly to Christ.
basic.god: God is shown as Creator and rightful owner of the whole earth, as the holy one who requires clean hands and a pure heart of those who would approach Him, and as the triumphant King of glory, strong and mighty, worthy of the grandest possible welcome.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Samuel 6:12-15 records David bringing the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem, the probable original setting of this psalm. 1 Corinthians 2:8 and James 2:1 both call Jesus the Lord of glory, applying this psalm's title directly to Him. Ephesians 4:8-10 describes Christ's ascension far above the heavens.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's declaration that the whole earth belongs to the LORD, its entrance question requiring clean hands and a pure heart, and its climactic call for the ancient gates to admit the King of glory together anticipate the whole gospel story's completion: Christ's triumphant ascension and enthronement as the true King of glory, who alone grants sinners clean hands and a pure heart through His own righteousness.

context.literary:
Psalm 24 is built around questions, and the questions order its three movements. Verses 1 and 2 are a statement with no question at all, a confession about who owns the world. Verse 3 then asks, 'Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place?' and verses 4 to 6 answer. Verses 7 to 10 ask twice, 'Who is this King of Glory?' and answer each time by naming Him. The psalm moves from a fact, to a question about people, to a question about God, and the first question about who may come up is answered by the second, since the one who fills the gates is the one people are hoping to reach.

The pivot between the second and third movements is a single verb. In Hebrew the verb 'lift' runs through the middle of the psalm. The one who may ascend is the man who 'does not lift up his soul to an idol,' verse 4. He will 'receive,' literally 'lift,' a blessing, verse 5. The gates are then told to 'lift up' their heads, verse 7, and the doors to 'be lifted up.' The same root carries the moral demand, the reward and the procession. A person who lifts his soul to the LORD alone is the person who will lift a blessing away, and the gates that lift their heads let the King in. The poem is stitched together by that one word.

The psalm also has a second stitching, the repeated 'seek.' The generation of verse 6 is 'those who seek Him,' and the phrase is doubled: 'who seek Your face.' The face of God is then what appears at the gates, in a King whose glory is His visible weight. To seek God's face and to see His glory in procession are the same longing, one from the human side and one from God's.

The last section is the most dramatic. Verses 7 and 9 are identical apart from the connecting phrase, and verses 8 and 10 answer them, first 'The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle,' then 'The LORD of Hosts.' The repeated call builds. The first answer describes the King as a warrior, and the second names Him with the title that means the commander of every host in heaven and on earth. The final 'He is the King of Glory' is the psalm's last word, before a closing Selah.

The psalm has a hidden symmetry with the great creation hymns. It begins at the foundations of the earth and ends at the doors of the city. What is founded upon the seas at the start is entered by the King at the close, so the whole world is His before He arrives at His house.
context.historical:
Psalm 24 carries the heading 'A Psalm of David,' and the natural setting is the day David brought the ark up to Jerusalem. The account in 2 Samuel 6 says that 'he and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and the sounding of the ram's horn,' 2 Samuel 6:15, and 1 Chronicles 15:25 to 28 adds the musicians, the linen robes and the sacrifices. The ark was the throne on which the LORD sat, 'enthroned between the cherubim,' 2 Samuel 6:2, and it was known as the place of His name. When the ark moved, God was understood to move. The first line of Israel's marching song for it was 'Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered,' Numbers 10:35. That explains why the King in the gates is a warrior in verse 8.

Psalm 132:7 to 9 shows that this kind of procession became a pattern in Israel's worship. 'Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool,' the pilgrims sing, and they ask God to arise to His resting place, 'You and the ark of Your strength.' The processions may well have been repeated at festivals, with priests and Levites carrying the ark or its symbol up the mountain and a singer or choir at the gate responding. That is why the two views on the psalm's origin, one historical event or a recurrent rite, are not as far apart as they sound.

Jerusalem's hill was called 'the hill of the LORD.' Pilgrims went up to it, and 'ascend' was the ordinary verb for going to Jerusalem. The questions of verse 3 were familiar in the entrance liturgies of Israel. Psalm 15 asks almost the same thing, 'O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?' and answers with a list of conduct. Isaiah 33:14 to 16 does the same with the fear of the 'consuming fire' in Zion. A priest at the gate would ask, and the worshipper would answer, before entering.

Verse 1 would have sounded bold in a world where people held that each land belonged to its own deity. Israel's poet says the whole earth and everything in it is the LORD's, and Exodus 19:5 grounds Israel's election in that fact: 'for the whole earth is Mine.' The election of one people is not the choosing of one god among many. It comes from the God who owns everything.

The picture of the earth 'founded upon the seas' reflects an ancient way of picturing the world, land standing above the waters that the Creator had pushed back, Genesis 1:9 to 10. The seas were also for Israel a symbol of chaos, Psalm 93:3 to 4, and to say that God had fixed the land upon them was to say that chaos was already beneath His feet.
context.canonical:
Psalm 24 sits inside a clear cluster in Book One. Psalm 22 is the sufferer, Psalm 23 the Shepherd, and Psalm 24 the King in glory. Psalms 15 and 24 are the two great entrance liturgies, and the pairing invites readers to ask the same question from two sides. Psalm 15 asks who may dwell in God's tent and gives a list of conduct, while Psalm 24 asks who may ascend God's hill and then shows the King who is coming down to meet them.

Its opening declaration is taken up again and again. Deuteronomy 10:14 says the heavens and the earth 'and everything in it' belong to the LORD, and Psalm 50:12 says that God does not need Israel's sacrifices, since 'the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof.' Psalm 89:11 repeats it, 'The earth and its fullness You founded.' The New Testament applies it in a striking place. Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 10:26, 'The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof,' to settle a question about food sold in the market. Because everything belongs to God, a believer may eat without anxiety. The BSB footnote to verse 1 records the citation.

The entrance question and its answer echo through the Old Testament. Psalm 73:13 shows a poet who kept his heart pure and washed his hands in innocence and did not see the point, and Psalm 26:6 uses the washing of hands as a picture of coming to the altar. Isaiah 33:15 to 16 gives the same portrait of the person who may dwell on the heights. The Sermon on the Mount takes verse 4 into the beatitudes: 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God,' Matthew 5:8, which is very close to the promise that those who seek His face will be blessed.

The question 'Who is this King of Glory?' recurs in the New Testament as 'Lord of glory.' Paul says that the rulers of the age would not have crucified 'the Lord of glory' had they understood, 1 Corinthians 2:8. Stephen calls the Lord 'the God of glory,' Acts 7:2, which echoes Psalm 29:3. Hebrews 4:14 says that we have 'a great high priest who has passed through the heavens,' and Hebrews 9:24 that He 'entered heaven itself.' Ephesians 4:8 to 10 speaks of the ascension in words from Psalm 68:18 and not from Psalm 24, so the link to Psalm 24 is by theme and neighbourhood, but a strong one, since both psalms picture God going up in triumph with a procession.

The church fathers commonly read verses 7 to 10 of Christ's ascension into heaven, and later liturgies used the psalm on Ascension Day. That is a reading laid on the psalm from the New Testament's account, and it is a faithful one, though the psalm's first setting is the ark's entry.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet meant Israel to keep two truths together that were easy to separate. The first is that the LORD owns everything. The second is that He is holy and that not everyone may come near Him. A people who believe only the first could think the God of the whole earth is available to anyone on any terms. A people who believe only the second could think that God belongs to the temple. Verses 1 and 2 and verses 3 to 6 are set side by side to say that the owner of all is also the holy one, and that His presence has an entrance requirement.

The requirement is not a list of ritual details. Verse 4 gives four marks, hands, heart, soul and speech: clean hands, a pure heart, a soul not lifted to an idol, and no deceitful oath. The poet has gone straight to the whole person, action, motive, worship and word. The hearers were meant to notice that the one thing that would keep them out was not their ancestry or their offerings but their loyalty.

The promise of verse 5 is meant to reassure the honest worshipper: such a person 'will receive blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation.' What he receives is a gift, from a God who saves. The hearers were meant to hear grace in the phrase 'God of his salvation,' and to conclude that even the qualified person is qualified by a relationship, not by a record.

Verse 6 draws the boundary of the people. The phrase 'the generation of those who seek Him' defines belonging by seeking and not by mere birth, and by naming Jacob the poet points to Israel itself. Israel is meant to understand itself as a company of seekers.

The final scene is the answer to the whole psalm. Israel has asked who may come up, and now the poet lets them see who comes. The King they have been longing to meet is coming to them, at the head of a procession, through their own gates. The hearers were meant to lift their heads and welcome Him, and to see that the God who requires clean hands is also the God who comes to meet unclean people at the door.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what was sung at a procession and what the temple's gatekeepers asked of pilgrims. It does not lay down a checklist for salvation, and it should not be read as though a person might climb to God by keeping the four marks of verse 4. Psalm 73:13 shows that clean hands can be held up as a claim that God had failed to reward. Paul says that 'all have sinned and fall short,' Romans 3:23, and that God 'justifies the ungodly,' Romans 4:5. The psalm's entrance question is a real question, and its true answer is found in the One who satisfies it.

What is prescriptive is the pairing of ownership and holiness. We are told that the earth is the LORD's, so that nothing in creation is outside His claim, and we are told that worship requires a whole life, hands, heart, soul and word. Both remain binding. The New Testament uses the first with care: Paul's application in 1 Corinthians 10:26 releases believers from anxiety about food, and its limit is love for a weaker brother, 1 Corinthians 10:28 to 29.

The procession itself is a description of a worship event, not a command to march an ark. The church does not carry the ark, but it does gather to welcome the King, and it still asks the questions of verses 3 and 8.

The gates section warns against two errors. It cannot simply be read as a prediction with every detail fitted to the ascension, since the psalm has a life in Israel's own worship. And it should not be reduced to a piece of ancient ceremony without a larger claim. The New Testament shows that the King who entered the gates of Jerusalem in that procession has entered heaven itself, Hebrews 9:24.

debates.question: What occasion, if any, lies behind verses 7 to 10?

views.label: David's bringing the ark to Jerusalem
views.case: The heading names David, and 2 Samuel 6:15 describes a joyful procession with shouting and horns. The ark was God's throne, and the song addresses the gates of the city it is entering. The warrior title of verse 8 fits the ark's old role in battle, Numbers 10:35.

views.label: A recurring festival liturgy, or Solomon's dedication of the temple
views.case: The call and response is built to be repeated, and Psalm 132 shows that such processions were part of Israel's worship. The 'ancient doors' fit an established sanctuary as well as a new one. On this reading the psalm was sung over many years and its first use is not recoverable.

views.label: A hymn without a specific event, acted out in worship
views.case: The psalm gives no name or date. Some readers suggest that its dramatic form is a liturgical drama and that trying to pin it to one day claims more than the text gives. The text supports this caution.

debates.bearing: The psalm's theology does not depend on the answer, since in each case a worshipping people greets the LORD as a King entering His city.

debates.question: Is Psalm 24 one poem or two joined together?

views.label: Two originally separate poems
views.case: Verses 1 to 6 are a hymn with an entrance liturgy, and verses 7 to 10 are a processional song about the gates. The change of style and speaker is abrupt, and in verse 6 the address to God ends in a Selah. Some scholars suggest that the two were joined by an editor because they suit the same procession.

views.label: A single liturgy
views.case: The keyword 'lift' in verses 4, 5, 7 and 9 runs across the divide, as does the seeking of the face. The questions of verses 3 and 8 are answered in matching form. The psalm is a coherent script in which the worshippers ask who may ascend, then meet the One who ascends.

debates.bearing: Read as one, the psalm's movement from the earth to the gates gains force. Read as two, the editor's placing of them still says the same thing.

debates.question: How does the demand for clean hands and a pure heart square with grace?

views.label: It states the character of true worshippers, who are transformed by God
views.case: The psalm speaks of a person who receives blessing and vindication from 'the God of his salvation,' verse 5, and the description belongs to those who already seek Him. The prayer of Psalm 51:10, 'Create in me a clean heart, O God,' shows that the clean heart is God's gift, not the worshipper's achievement.

views.label: It states an ideal that shows the need for a mediator
views.case: The standard is so high that no one meets it, so the psalm drives the reader to ask who can. The New Testament answers that Christ is 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' Hebrews 7:26, and that we come by His blood with hearts sprinkled clean, Hebrews 10:19 to 22. On this reading the question of verse 3 finds its answer in Him.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the requirement is real and that God supplies what He requires. The New Testament makes the second explicit.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says that the earth is the LORD's 'and the fullness thereof.' The Hebrew word for fullness, melo, means all that fills something, the whole contents, and it pairs with 'world,' tevel, the inhabited earth, so that the verse first names the ground and then all that lives on it. The verse ends with 'all who dwell therein,' so that people are counted as part of the LORD's possessions.

Verse 2 says that He founded it 'upon the seas' and established it 'upon the waters.' The second word is normally translated 'rivers,' so the poet has set the two most common water words side by side. Psalm 93:3 speaks of rivers that have 'raised their voice,' and the same word for the surging of chaos appears there. The verbs are those of a builder, founding and making firm, so the Creator is pictured laying a foundation on the very things that Israel feared.

Verse 3 asks who may 'ascend,' the verb used for going up to Jerusalem, and who may 'stand' in His holy place. The two verbs go together, going up and standing, since it is one thing to reach the place and another to remain there.

In verse 4 the man has 'clean hands.' The Hebrew phrase is 'clean of hands' and it pairs with 'pure of heart,' bar, which speaks of purity that is free of mixture. The lifting of the soul is the key. The verb is nasa, and the object 'to an idol' is literally 'to emptiness.' The BSB footnote says the word can also be rendered 'to falsehood or to vanity.' That range matters: what the worshipper refuses to lift his soul toward is anything hollow. The oath he will not swear is 'deceitfully,' with a word for treachery and fraud.

In verse 5 he will 'receive,' literally 'lift,' blessing. The same verb runs through the psalm and it is impossible to miss in Hebrew. The 'vindication' is tsedaqah, the word for righteousness, so he receives righteousness from the God of his salvation, which is a gift and not a wage.

Verse 6 says 'Such is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O God of Jacob.' The BSB footnote notes that the Septuagint, the Syriac and two Hebrew manuscripts read 'O God of Jacob,' while the Masoretic Text reads 'who seek your face, O Jacob.' On the second reading Jacob is a name for the people, the company of seekers, and the psalm addresses Israel as the seeker. Both readings are intelligible, and the difference lies in whether Jacob is the one addressed or the God whose face is sought.

Verse 7 calls on the 'gates' to lift their heads and on the 'ancient doors,' literally the doors of eternity or of long ago, to be lifted. The verb of the second clause is a passive form of the same nasa. The gates are personified, and the poet commands them as though they might be too low for what is coming.

The title 'King of Glory,' melekh hakavod, uses the noun kavod, from the root for 'heavy.' Glory is the weight of a person, the presence that cannot be ignored. Psalm 29:3 calls Him 'the God of glory' who thunders over the waters, and Isaiah 6:3 says that the whole earth is full of His glory. Verse 8 says He is 'strong and mighty,' with a pair of adjectives for strength, and 'mighty in battle,' echoing Exodus 15:3, 'The LORD is a warrior.'

The final title in verse 10, 'the LORD of Hosts,' tseva'ot, means the armies of heaven and of Israel. It is the title tied to the ark in 2 Samuel 6:2, where the ark is 'the name of the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim.' The gates are opened to the God whose name goes with the ark.

typology.type: The one who may ascend the hill, verses 3 and 4
typology.fulfillment: The psalm asks who has clean hands and a pure heart and gives no name. The New Testament names Him. 'He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, and He is 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' Hebrews 7:26. The One who satisfies the entrance question also takes His people with Him: 'we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus,' Hebrews 10:19, with 'hearts sprinkled to cleanse us,' verse 22. The type falls short because no Israelite fully met the requirement, so the priests' questions could only point ahead.

typology.type: The ark entering the city, verses 7 to 10
typology.fulfillment: The ark was the visible sign of God's throne, and its procession into Jerusalem showed God coming to live with His people. John says, 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, using the language of the tabernacle. The ark was a small and passing sign of a presence that was later found in a person. The escalation is that God does not merely dwell in a box carried by Levites but takes human nature. The type falls short because the ark could be captured and lost, while the Son cannot.

typology.type: The gates lifted for the King, verses 7 and 9
typology.fulfillment: The gates that lift their heads are a picture of every barrier giving way. In the ascension, Jesus 'was taken up' as the disciples watched, Acts 1:9, and Peter says that He has gone into heaven 'with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him,' 1 Peter 3:22. Paul says that God 'seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms, far above all rule and authority,' Ephesians 1:20 to 21. Hebrews adds that He 'entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf,' Hebrews 9:24. The type falls short because Jerusalem's gates were stone, and the powers of heaven are those He has overcome.

typology.type: The King mighty in battle, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The King who enters is a warrior. In Christ, the battle was fought at the cross, where God, 'having disarmed the powers and authorities, made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross,' Colossians 2:15. The picture of a returning victor is real, and Paul sees the same triumph in the ascension of Ephesians 4:8, 'He led captives away.' The correspondence holds between the warrior LORD and the Son who wins, though the weapon is a death. The type falls short in that the ark's wars were fought with armies, while His victory is won through weakness.

study.christ:
Psalm 24 leads to Christ in three ways, each with a firm footing in the New Testament. First, it asks a question that only He answers. 'Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place?' The description of the person with clean hands, a pure heart and a soul lifted to no idol is a portrait no other person fits. The New Testament calls Christ the one who 'committed no sin,' 1 Peter 2:22, and 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' Hebrews 7:26. The psalm therefore speaks a truth that its first hearers could feel and not yet satisfy: the hill can be climbed only by a person who is clean, and the One who is clean has climbed it, on behalf of the unclean. Hebrews puts it as a forerunner: 'where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf,' Hebrews 6:20, and it says that He 'entered heaven itself,' Hebrews 9:24. His people follow through His blood, 'having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us,' Hebrews 10:22, and the pure in heart 'will see God,' Matthew 5:8.

Second, it leads to Christ through the title 'King of Glory.' Paul writes that the rulers of this age 'would not have crucified the Lord of glory,' 1 Corinthians 2:8, and by using the title he places Jesus as the one at the gates. The Old Testament title is thus given to the crucified. The connection is unsettling in the best way: the glory that filled the ark's procession and the gates was the glory of the man on the cross. When John writes that 'we have seen His glory,' John 1:14, he means that the King has come through the gates in human flesh.

Third, it leads to Christ in His ascension, which is the traditional reading of the church. Luke describes Jesus being taken up, Acts 1:9. Peter adds that He has 'gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him,' 1 Peter 3:22, and Paul that God has seated Him 'far above all rule and authority, power and dominion,' Ephesians 1:20 to 21. Nothing here quotes Psalm 24, and Ephesians 4:8 quotes Psalm 68:18, but the pictures agree: a warrior returns in triumph and takes His place, and a heavenly city receives Him. The welcome the gates owe Him is given in Revelation 5:12, where the crowds around the throne say that the slain Lamb is 'worthy to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!'

There is a fitting pattern to the way the Psalter places this psalm after the cross of Psalm 22 and the Shepherd of Psalm 23. The Man who was pierced and who leads through the dark valley is the King who comes through the gates, and these are not three people but one.

Two cautions keep the reading honest. The psalm was sung first at a procession of the ark, and the church's reading rests on the New Testament's account of Christ's ascension and not on a claim that the psalm was written only for it. And we should not turn every detail into a code. The gates need not be particular heavenly gates. What the passage gives the church is the shape of the event: the holy King, worthy of the grandest welcome, comes in, and He brings people with Him.
study.god:
The psalm begins with God as Owner. Everything is His: the land, its contents, the people, the depths on which the land rests. Nothing is neutral ground. That includes the believer's own life, and the doctrine of creation here is not a piece of cosmology but a statement about who has the right to ask for everything. The verb 'founded' also says that the LORD is the builder, so what He owns He first made.

The psalm then shows God as holy, and His holiness is stated as a boundary. Someone may ascend, and someone may not. The hill is His, the place is His holy place, and He decides who stands there. The God who owns the whole earth is not thereby the God of every human project. His holiness is a fact about Him, and the psalm sets the matching requirement in the moral life of the worshipper: hands, heart, soul, word. It shows that holiness for God means a wholeness that He asks of those who come close.

It shows God as a giver of blessing and righteousness, verse 5. The worshipper does not earn a wage but receives, and the phrase 'the God of his salvation' says that the blessing comes from a Saviour. This corrects any reading of the entrance requirement as bare law. The God who asks for clean hands is the God who supplies righteousness to those who seek Him.

The psalm shows God as King and as warrior. The titles in verse 8, 'strong and mighty' and 'mighty in battle,' are not decorative. This King fights, and He wins. The Old Testament did not shy from calling God a warrior, Exodus 15:3, and the psalm gives that title a setting of glad welcome. His strength is not the threat but the reason for the celebration, since the enemies of His people are the ones He defeats. In the light of the New Testament the battle is the cross, Colossians 2:15.

It shows God as present. The entire third movement is about arrival. The King is not far off, and He is entering His people's city. Psalm 132:14 has God say, 'This is My resting place forever and ever; here I will dwell,' and Psalm 24 sings of the day He comes in. The God of the whole earth chooses a place to live among a particular people, which is the mystery that John 1:14 finally explains.

There is a tension the psalm holds together. God is transcendent, since He is Lord of the seas and the earth, and He is near, since He comes through the gates. He is holy, and He welcomes those who seek Him. He is glory, weight that no one can carry, and He is a King who listens to those who lift their heads.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to begin with what is His, to ask honestly who may come, to seek His face, and to lift our heads when He arrives. Believers lift the gates of their hearts and of their days, and the King of Glory comes in.

crossReferences.note: The nearest twin of Psalm 24:3 to 6. It asks who may abide in God's tent or dwell on His holy mountain, and answers with a list of conduct. Set beside Psalm 24, it shows that Israel had a standard question at the door of worship and that character, not birth, decided the reply.

Paul quotes verse 1, 'The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof,' to tell the Corinthians that they may eat what is sold in the market. Because all things belong to God, no food is ritually tainted. The BSB footnote marks the citation, and the verse shows how large the psalm's first line is.

God tells Israel that they will be His treasured possession out of all nations, 'for the whole earth is Mine.' It states the claim of Psalm 24:1 at the moment of Israel's election. Chosen status is grounded in universal ownership, not in the belittling of other peoples.

When the ark set out, Moses said, 'Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered.' It explains why the King of Psalm 24:8 is 'mighty in battle.' The ark's marching song was a war cry, and its entry into Jerusalem was the arrival of a victorious God.

The ark is called by the name of 'the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim.' The title in Psalm 24:10 is here tied to the ark itself, which supports the reading that the psalm was sung at its procession. The gates are opened to the God whose throne is carried in.

Pilgrims sing, 'Let us go to His dwelling place,' and ask God to arise to His resting place with the ark. It shows that processions with the ark were part of Israel's festival worship and gives a plausible setting for Psalm 24 as something sung more than once.

The rivers raise their voice, and the floodwaters rise, but 'the LORD on high is majestic' above them. It explains why Psalm 24:2 says that the earth is founded on seas and rivers. In Israel's poetry those waters stood for chaos, and the Creator sits above them.

'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.' Jesus takes the second mark of Psalm 24:4 and attaches the promise of seeing God, which is the goal of those who seek His face in verse 6. He presents inner purity as the true reading of the psalm's entrance question.

Such a high priest is 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.' The description matches the person Psalm 24:4 asks for. The writer says that the ascender the psalm needed has come, and that He is also the priest who brings others in.

'We have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus,' with 'hearts sprinkled to cleanse us.' It answers how the unclean may ascend the hill. The clean heart that Psalm 24 requires is given through His blood, and the approach is made in full assurance.

The rulers of this age would not have crucified 'the Lord of glory' had they understood. The title of Psalm 24:7 to 10 is used of Jesus, and Paul thereby announces that the glorious King of the gates is the one who was crucified. The two seem opposites, and Paul holds them together.

Christ 'has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him.' It supplies the New Testament's own picture of the King who enters and takes His throne, which is the reading the church has given the gates of Psalm 24.

The city's gates 'will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there.' The gates that once had to be lifted for the King now stand open forever, and the people who enter are those whose names are in the Lamb's Book of Life.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 24 begins with the opening of the Bible. Genesis 1 says that God gathered the waters and made the dry land appear, and verse 2 says that He founded the earth on the seas. The claim that the earth is the LORD's is the claim of Genesis 1 made in a song. The rest of the psalm then asks what became of the creation's owner and its tenants, since Genesis 3 shows the tenants driven from His presence, east of Eden, with cherubim guarding the way back. The question 'Who may ascend the hill of the LORD?' is the question of the whole Bible: who can come back?

In the Old Testament the answer is given in picture and promise. Israel is given a hill, a tent and then a temple, and the priests ask at the door who may enter. The ark of God, with cherubim on its cover, comes to rest among them, and the psalm sings of its arrival. The presence that was lost at Eden is restored in symbol, but the symbol is guarded. Psalm 15 and Psalm 24 show the fence, and the history of Israel shows how few kept the condition. The prophets say the same about Zion, that the ungodly cannot dwell with a consuming fire, Isaiah 33:14.

The psalm sets up what follows. It shows the King coming, and it leaves open who will be enough to stand in His holy place. Israel's king is the obvious candidate, and the Psalter's kings all fall short. The story then goes to the Servant and to the Son of David whose kingdom will not end. In Christ the two halves of the psalm meet. The One with clean hands and a pure heart ascends the hill, and the King of Glory enters the gates. He does this at the cross and in the resurrection, and then in the ascension, when He 'entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf,' Hebrews 9:24.

The consequence is that His people come in with Him. The way through the curtain has been opened, Hebrews 10:19 to 20, and the people who seek His face are the company of Psalm 24:6, a generation drawn from every nation and not only from Jacob. The church still asks, and still answers, in the words of the psalm, while the gates wait.

In the new creation the psalm is fulfilled entire. The earth is filled with the LORD's glory, and the nations bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. The gates are never shut, Revelation 21:25, and the throne of God and of the Lamb is within the city, and 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. What the psalm asks in verse 6, to seek His face, ends at last in seeing it. The King who once entered through gates lifted for Him now lives with His people, and there is no further hill to climb.

quiz.q: What does the psalm declare about the earth in verses 1-2?

options.text: That the earth and everyone in it belongs to the LORD, who founded it upon the seas and waters.
options.note: This opening declaration of God's total ownership grounds the psalm's entire message.

options.text: That the earth belongs jointly to all its human inhabitants equally.
options.note: The psalm attributes ownership specifically and solely to the LORD, not to humanity collectively.

options.text: That the earth is eternal and uncreated.
options.note: The psalm explicitly describes God founding and establishing the earth, implying it is created, not uncreated.

options.text: That only Israel's specific territory belongs to God, not the whole earth.
options.note: The psalm's language is universal, the earth and its fullness, not limited to a specific territory.

quiz.q: How does verse 4 answer the entrance question of who may ascend the LORD's hill?

options.text: The one who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not worship idols or swear deceitfully.
options.note: This ethical portrait closely parallels the answer given in Psalm 15.

options.text: Only those born into the priestly tribe of Levi.
options.note: The psalm's criteria are ethical and spiritual, not based on tribal descent.

options.text: Anyone who has offered the required number of sacrifices.
options.note: The psalm's answer centers on inward purity and honest dealing, not a quota of sacrifices.

options.text: Those who possess the greatest material wealth.
options.note: The psalm's criteria concern moral and spiritual purity, not material wealth.

quiz.q: What dramatic scene unfolds in verses 7-10?

options.text: A call for ancient gates and doors to lift up their heads so the King of glory may enter, followed by the repeated question, who is this King of glory.
options.note: This antiphonal call and response forms the psalm's dramatic, triumphant climax.

options.text: A description of the destruction of Jerusalem's gates by an invading army.
options.note: The scene describes gates being lifted up in triumphant welcome, not destroyed by an enemy.

options.text: A private prayer offered silently by a single worshiper.
options.note: The scene is public, dramatic, and communal, likely antiphonal between two choirs, not a private, silent prayer.

options.text: A list of specific temple furnishings and their measurements.
options.note: This is unrelated to the psalm's actual content, which is a triumphant procession scene, not architectural measurements.

quiz.q: How is the King of glory identified in verses 8 and 10?

options.text: As the LORD, strong and mighty, mighty in battle, and the LORD of Hosts.
options.note: Both answers to the repeated question name the LORD Himself with titles of strength and command.

options.text: As an unnamed future prophet.
options.note: The psalm names the King of glory explicitly as the LORD, not an unnamed prophet.

options.text: As the reigning human king of Israel at the time.
options.note: While a human king may have led the procession, the psalm's answer identifies the King of glory as the LORD Himself, not merely the human monarch.

options.text: As a foreign king conquering Jerusalem.
options.note: The scene celebrates the LORD's triumphant entrance, not a foreign conqueror's invasion.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament apply this psalm's title, King of glory or Lord of glory, to Christ?

options.text: Paul calls Jesus 'the Lord of glory' in 1 Corinthians 2:8, and James calls Him 'our glorious Lord Jesus Christ' in James 2:1, both using this psalm's exact title.
options.note: These direct New Testament uses of the title show the earliest church applying this psalm's climactic language to Christ.

options.text: The New Testament never applies any title from this psalm to Jesus.
options.note: This is incorrect; both Paul and James explicitly use the title Lord of glory for Jesus.

options.text: It is applied only to God the Father, never to Jesus.
options.note: The New Testament passages cited apply the title specifically and directly to Jesus Christ.

options.text: It is applied only in a symbolic sense with no real theological weight.
options.note: The title carries substantial theological weight, affirming Christ's full deity and glory, not a merely symbolic use.

questions: This psalm declares that the whole earth, not just sacred spaces, belongs to the LORD. How does remembering that everything you have and everywhere you go already belongs to God change the way you use your time, money, or possessions this week?

The entrance question asks for clean hands and a pure heart. Where do you sense your own hands or heart are not clean right now, and how do you need to bring that honestly before God rather than hiding it?

The psalm pictures a dramatic, joyful procession welcoming the King of glory. What would it look like for your own approach to worship this week to carry more of that sense of anticipation and celebration rather than routine?

The question 'Who is this King of glory' is asked twice and answered each time by naming God's strength and might. When you think about who God is, do strength and might come to mind readily, or do you tend to picture Him in smaller, more manageable terms?

The New Testament applies this exact title, Lord of glory, directly to Jesus. How does calling Jesus by this exalted, powerful title shape the way you pray to Him or trust Him with what currently feels too big for you to handle?

translationNotes.note: Selah likely marks a pause for reflection or musical interlude, appearing here after the description of those who seek God's face.
Lift up your heads, O gates pictures ancient city gates personified, called to open wide enough and high enough for a great and glorious king's procession to enter.
King of Glory renders King of kavod, a title Paul and James both apply directly to Jesus Christ in the New Testament.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Psalm 24:1-10.
